newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Herzog promises Holocaust compensation for Hungary.
newsitem.headline: Herzog promises Holocaust compensation for Hungary.

text.p: Visiting German President Roman Herzog said on Wednesday he was sure an agreement would be signed with Hungary on compensation for Holocaust survivors "within a very short time".
"Essential steps are now necessary and I am sure that within a short time a mutual agreement will be reached," Herzog told journalists on the second day of a three-day official visit to Hungary.
Herzog added that if compensation had been paid before 1989 to a communist government much of it would not have reached the victims.
"One has to take into account that the communist system would have taken the money and the victims would not have seen very much of it," he said.
On Tuesday a group of around 100 Jewish Holocaust survivors staged a protest for compensation as Herzog visited Budapest's main synagogue.
A grim-faced Herzog inmmediately went over to the protesters who stood quietly behind barriers and assured them they would receive payment.
One protester, Helen Fecher, 73, who spent one and a half years in Nazi death camps, expressed frustration that the process of compensation was taking so long.
"There are so few of us left the longer they take the less they have to pay," she told Reuters. "They're paying their retired people plenty but we get nothing."

An estimated half a million Jews and Gypsies were deported from Hungary to Auschwitz and other Nazi death camps from March 1944 until the end of the World War Two in May 1945. Only a few thousand returned.
Herzog said he envisaged an accord that would be in line with existing agreements with Poland, Belarus, Ukraine and most recently the Czech republic.

Bonn signed last month a landmark joint post-war act of contrition with Prague, drawn up after two years of delicate talks, in which Germany expresses its sorrow for the Nazi occupation of the Czech lands between 1938 and 1945.
Herzog's visit to Hungary is being dominated by the issue of the treatment of minorities.
On Wednesday morning the German president, attending a roundtable conference on Hungary's national and ethnic minorities, described Hungary's legislation on minority rights as "exemplary".
Hungary's Secretary of State responsible for minority affairs Csaba Tabajdi thanked Herzog for the financial and moral help Germany gives its ethnic kin in Hungary.
"With Hungary, 200,000 Germans will join the European Union," he said, referring to Herzog's comments on Tuesday that he was sure Hungary would be among the first to join the European Union.
Herzog went on to visit the 7,000-strong German-speaking village of Solymar, near Budapest and laid a wreath at a monument to the deportation in 1946 of thousands of ethnic Germans from Hungary.

"There were also German victims of the war," said Herzog, adding that he had been impressed by the determination of the ethnic German community of Solymar, which lost a quarter of its population in the 1946 deporations, to put the past behind them.
Herzog will end his visit on Thursday by touring Hungary's economically depressed eastern region centred around the towns of Nyiregyhaza and Debrecen.
"We can see economic development has gone much further in the west of the country than in the east," he said.
"We want to express our interest in the whole of Hungary -- we will see what is needed and what we can do," he said.
